### theme_quarto() and theme_manuscript()

I created my own themes to add to figures. `theme_quarto()` is used to add themes to figures as displayed in the Quarto document and saved to disk as `.pdf` or `.png`. `theme_manuscript()` is used to add themes to figures as they will end up in the manuscript. I can already add arguments with `theme()` or specific themes (e.g. `theme_classic()`, my personal favourite) to plots; adding `theme()` afterwards keeps whatever was added in `theme()` before it, unless I specify that arugment here - that's why I allowed to specify some things within my functions as well.

```{r}
#| label: chunk-05-helper-themes
theme_quarto <- function(
    legend_position = "right", 
    plot_title = element_blank()
    ) {
    theme(
      plot.title = plot_title,
      legend.position = legend_position
    )
}

theme_manuscript <- function(
    legend_position = "none",
    plot_title = element_blank(),
    axis_title_size = 8,
    axis_text_size = 6
    ) {
    theme(
      plot.title = plot_title,
      legend.position = legend_position,
      axis.title = element_text(size = axis_title_size),
      axis.text = element_text(size = axis_text_size),
      legend.key.size = unit(0.4, "cm"), 
      legend.text = element_text(size = 8),
      legend.title = element_text(size = 9)
    )
}

```

### save_plot()

This document displays all the figures I make, but I also want them saved to disk — both as `.png` and `.pdf`. I only need to provide the ggplot object, a filename (without extension), and optionally the width and height of the figure and additional arguments put into themes.

The figures for my written report contain subfigures spread across multiple scripts. Since I want to assemble these panel figures via R code rather than by hand, `save_plot()` can also optionally save the plot object itself to disk as an .rds file, for a final script to later combine with `patchwork`. Set figure to the name the figure should carry in the report (e.g. `"SF1A"`) to trigger this; leave it `NULL` (the default) to just save the `.png`/`.pdf` as normal.

A live ggplot object carries its underlying data along with it — for plots built from large Seurat objects, this can balloon the saved file to gigabytes. To avoid this, `save_plot()` converts the object to a grob (a static, pre-rendered drawing, with no data attached) before saving it as `.rds`. This is controlled by the `grob` argument, and defaults to `TRUE`, since converting a small plot costs nothing but forgetting to convert a large one is expensive. Set `grob = FALSE` only if a later step specifically needs the original, live ggplot object rather than its rendered form.

```{r}
#| label: chunk-06-helper-save-plot
save_plot <- function(
    p, filename, 
    width = 10, height = 6, 
    figure = NULL, grob = TRUE, apply_theme = TRUE, 
    add_tag = TRUE, tag_text_size = 14,
    legend_pos_manuscript = "none"
    ) {
  ## Save image on disk as png and pdf
  # Add Quarto-specific theme, unless the plot has its own custom theme
  if (apply_theme) {
    p_image <- p + theme_quarto()
  } else {
    p_image <- p
  }
  file_png <- file.path(dir_fig, paste0(filename, ".png"))
  ggsave(file_png, p_image, width = width, height = height, dpi = 150)
  file_pdf <- file.path(dir_fig, paste0(filename, ".pdf"))
  ggsave(file_pdf, p_image, width = width, height = height, dpi = 150)
  
  ## Save the ggplot object on disk as an rds file 
  if (!is.null(figure)) {
    # Add tag if needed
    if (add_tag) {
      tag <- str_extract(figure, "[A-Z]$")
      p <- p + 
        labs(tag = tag) + 
        theme(
          plot.tag = element_text(
            face = "bold", 
            size = tag_text_size, 
            hjust = 0, vjust = 0
            )
        )
    }
    # Add manuscript-specific theme, unless the plot has its own custom theme
    if (apply_theme) {
      p <- p + theme_manuscript(legend_position = legend_pos_manuscript)
    }
    file_rds <- file.path(dir_man, paste0(figure, ".rds"))
    # Convert the object to a grob if needed
    if (grob) {
      p <- ggplotGrob(p)
    }
    # Save on disk
    saveRDS(p, file_rds)
  }
}
```

### print_tabset()

Quarto cannot cross-reference figures that are made inside a loop. To still display the plots of a loop in this document, I collect them in a named list and show them as tabs with `print_tabset()`. The names of the list become the tab titles. It also accepts data frames (shown as a table). This function writes raw Quarto markdown, so the chunk that calls it needs the chunk option `#| output: asis`. `heading_level` should be one deeper than the heading above the chunk.

```{r}
#| label: chunk-07-helper-print-tabset
print_tabset <- function(obj_list, heading_level = 3) {
  cat("::: {.panel-tabset}\n\n")
  for (nm in names(obj_list)) {
    cat(strrep("#", heading_level), " ", nm, "\n\n", sep = "")
    obj <- obj_list[[nm]]
    if (inherits(obj, "ggplot")) {
      print(obj)
    } else if (is.data.frame(obj)) {
      cat(knitr::kable(obj, format = "pipe"), sep = "\n")
    }
    cat("\n\n")
  }
  cat(":::\n\n")
}
```


### variable_feature_selection()

I want to remove sex chromosome genes and mitochondrial genes in the FindVariableFeatures step. This does not remove these genes from all further analysis, but it just prevents these genes from affecting dimensionality reduction and subsequent clustering. As this involves quite a lot of steps, I decided to write a function, instead of running all these lines in a chunk below.

You need to provide the Seurat object and a vector with the sex chromosome genes of your particular seurat object.

```{r}
#| label: chunk-08-helper-variable-feature-selection
variable_feature_selection <- function(seu, sexgenes) {
  # Create a vector of all genes
  genes <- rownames(seu@assays$RNA$counts)
  
  # Create a vector of mitochondrial genes
  mitogenes <- genes[grep("^MT-", genes)]
  
  # Create a new Seurat object with mitochondrial and sex chromosome genes removed
  genes_to_remove <- c(mitogenes, sexgenes)
  genes_boolean <- (genes %in% genes_to_remove)
  gene_selection_counts <- seu@assays$RNA$counts[!genes_boolean, ]
  gene_selection_seu_obj <- CreateSeuratObject(counts = gene_selection_counts)
  gene_selection_seu_obj <- NormalizeData(gene_selection_seu_obj)
  
  # Run variable feature selection on the gene-selected Seurat object
  gene_selection_seu_obj <- FindVariableFeatures(
    gene_selection_seu_obj,
    selection.method = "vst",
    nfeatures = 2000
  )
  # Create a vector of the variable features of the gene-selected Seurat object
  variable_features <- VariableFeatures(gene_selection_seu_obj)
  # Transfer variable features to main seurat object
  VariableFeatures(seu) <- variable_features
  
  # Remove the objects which are no longer needed to save memory
  rm(gene_selection_counts)
  rm(gene_selection_seu_obj)
  
  # Return the seurat object with variable features set
  seu
}
```

### top_markers()

I'll display the top genes for each cluster after running FindMarkers().

```{r}
#| label: chunk-09-helper-top-markers

top_markers <- function(markers, cluster_select = NULL, n_genes = 10) {
  if (!is.null(cluster_select)) {
      markers |>
        filter(cluster == cluster_select) |>
        filter(p_val_adj < 0.05) |>
        slice_max(avg_log2FC, n = n_genes)
  } else {
    stop("You did not provide a cluster to select")
  }
  
}
```

### prepare_gsea() and gsea_pathway_selection()

If the test `FindAllMarkers()` has been run, I need to subset a cluster, so the identity argument should provide what identity/cluster we are interested in. If the test `FindMarkers()` has been run, this is not a problem, but this does not automatically have a column gene; these are rownames and should become a column.

Two ways to sort: 
- `logfc`: directly by logfc
- `signed_logp`: -log10(p-value), with the sign (+/-) of the logFC

`gsea_pathway_selection()` is a quick little function which extracts the most upregulated and downregulated pathways of a FGSEA results table, mostly for visualization. The numbers for upregulated and downregulated pathways are defined in the "Define variables" section

```{r}
#| label: chunk-10-helpers-gsea

prepare_gsea <- function(markers, findallmarkers = FALSE, identity = NULL,
                         sort = "logfc") {
  if(findallmarkers) {
     markers <- markers |>
       filter(cluster == identity)
  } else {
    markers <- markers |>
      rownames_to_column(var = "gene")
  }
  # Remove non-SYMBOL genes
  markers <- filter(markers, !str_detect(gene, "ENSG"))

  # Sort genes based on selected sorting method
  if (sort != "logfc" & sort != "signed_logp") {
    stop("You did not select a valid sorting method")
  } else if (sort == "logfc") {
    # Rank by logFC
    markers <- arrange(markers, desc(avg_log2FC))
    # Extract a named vector of the ranked genes
    gene_scores <- markers$avg_log2FC
    names(gene_scores) <- markers$gene
  } else if (sort == "signed_logp") {
    markers <- markers |>
      mutate(
      rankings = sign(avg_log2FC)*(-log10(p_val_adj)),
      rankings = case_when(
        rankings == Inf ~ 350, # a little higher than maximum value
        rankings == -Inf ~ -350,
        .default = rankings
        )
      ) |>
      arrange(desc(rankings))
    # Extract a named vector of the ranked genes
    gene_scores <- markers$rankings
    names(gene_scores) <- markers$gene
  }

  gene_scores
}

gsea_pathway_selection <- function(gsea_results, n_up = 10, n_down = 0) {
  top_pathways_up <- gsea_results |> 
    filter(padj < 0.05) |>  
    slice_max(NES, n = n_up) |>
    pull(pathway)
  top_pathways_down <- gsea_results |>
    filter(padj < 0.05) |>
    slice_min(NES, n = n_down) |>
    pull(pathway)
  top_pathways <- c(top_pathways_up, rev(top_pathways_down))
  top_pathways
}
```

### boxplot_composition()

`boxplot_composition()` creates the visualizations of cell composition. The input is the dataframe cell_counts, which is created in the first chunk under the header "Cell Composition Analysis".

```{r}
#| label: chunk-11-helper-boxplot-composition
boxplot_composition <- function(cell_counts, variable = "AnonymousID") {
  # For ggplot2, I need to pivot longer, so that each count becomes a row
  cell_counts_ggplot <- cell_counts |> 
    mutate(
      total_counts = `GM Astrocyte` + `WM Astrocyte 1` + `WM Astrocyte 2`,
      `GM Astrocyte` = `GM Astrocyte` / total_counts,
      `WM Astrocyte 1` = `WM Astrocyte 1` / total_counts,
      `WM Astrocyte 2` = `WM Astrocyte 2` / total_counts
      ) |>
    pivot_longer(
      cols = c("GM Astrocyte", "WM Astrocyte 1", "WM Astrocyte 2"),
      names_to = "cellstate",
      values_to = "Proportion"
    )
  
  p_box <- ggplot(
    cell_counts_ggplot, 
    aes(x = cellstate, y= Proportion, fill = !!sym(variable))
    ) +
    geom_boxplot(alpha = 0.7) +
    geom_point(
      aes(group = !!sym(variable)), colour = "grey20", size = 0.6,
      position = position_jitterdodge(jitter.width = 0.4, dodge.width = 0.8)
      ) +
    theme_classic()
  
  p_box
}
```

## Standard Seurat processing (Normalize, Variable Features, PCA, UMAP, etc.)

I wanted to remove sex chromosome genes and mitochondrial genes in the FindVariableFeatures step and created the helper function variable_feature_selection() to do so. The vector `sexgenes` should be specific for the genes which are and which are not in your Seurat object, so when I wanted to do this, \[name\] shared a text file with me. In hindsight, this was not the most reproducible or neat approach, but it is what I did all those months ago, so I'll use it now as well. For transparancy, this sex_gene.txt file is also in the Git repo under `/data/metainformation/sex_genes.txt`.

```{r}
#| label: chunk-14-processing
seu <- NormalizeData(seu)

## Variable features -----------------------------------------------------------

# sex_genes.txt stores a list of sex genes in my seurat object 
file_txt <- file.path(dir_data_meta, "sex_genes.txt")
sexgenes <- read_table(file_txt, col_names = FALSE) |> pull(X1)

seu <- variable_feature_selection(seu, sexgenes)

## Further processing ----------------------------------------------------------

seu <- ScaleData(seu, vars.to.regress = "percent.mt")
seu <- RunPCA(seu) # Runs on variable features by default
seu <- RunHarmony(seu, group.by.vars = "AnonymousID")
# Seurat::RunUMAP sets a seed (seed.use = 42) by default, no need to do manually
seu <- RunUMAP(seu, reduction = "harmony", dims = 1:dims)
seu <- FindNeighbors(seu, reduction = "harmony", k.param = k, dims = 1:dims)


## Join layers again -----------------------------------------------------------


# [name] seperated layers per participant for preprocessing (especially
# normalization). Later steps needs joined layers, so join them together again.
seu <- JoinLayers(seu)
```

# Discrete cluster approach

## Clustering itself: Seurat's FindClusters()

I assessed multiple clustering resolutions and chose to continue with cluster resolution 0.15, as higher resolutions create clusters which are hardly distinguishable from one another and which flow into one other (the borders become a bit blurry). You could run this script again with a different resolution in the section "Defining variables", but subsequent sections regarding cluster annotation assume cluster resolution 0.15, so this might be a little buggy if one changes resolution.


```{r}
#| label: chunk-15-clustering
resolutions <- c(
  0.1, 0.15, 0.2, 0.25, 0.3, 0.35, 0.4,
  0.45, 0.5, 0.6, 0.8, 1.0
)

plots_clust_pca <- list()
plots_clust_umap <- list()
for (resolution in resolutions) {
  seu <- FindClusters(
    seu,
    resolution = resolution,
    cluster.name = paste0("seurat_cluster_res", resolution),
    algorithm = 4 # 4 = Leiden algorithm
    )
  title <- paste0("Resolution ", resolution)
  p_clust_pca <- DimPlot(
    seu, 
    reduction = "pca", 
    group.by = paste0("seurat_cluster_res", resolution),
    raster = TRUE,
    pt.size = 2,
    label = TRUE
  ) +
    theme_manuscript() +
    theme(plot.title = element_text(size = 10, face = "bold")) +
    labs(title = title)
  p_clust_umap <- DimPlot(
    seu, 
    reduction = "umap", 
    group.by = paste0("seurat_cluster_res", resolution),
    raster = TRUE,
    pt.size = 2,
    label = TRUE
  )  +
    theme_manuscript() +
    theme(plot.title = element_text(size = 10, face = "bold")) +
    labs(title = title)
  # Can only save resolution as a string
  list_entry_name <- paste0("res", resolution)
  plots_clust_pca[[list_entry_name]] <- p_clust_pca
  plots_clust_umap[[list_entry_name]] <- p_clust_umap
}
```

## Cluster interpretation and annotation

### Removal cluster 4

I removed cluster 4, because the markers of that cluster mostly were mitochondrial RNA. 

To find that, I first ran `FindAllMarkers()` for all clusters.

#### Seurat's FindAllMarkers()

I used Seurat's function `FindAllMarkers()` to interpret clusters. By default, `FindMarkers()` sets threshold for the minimum log-Fold Chance threshold (`logfc.threshold`) and minumum percentage of cells expressing the gene (`min.pct`). I am generally in favour of setting these thresholds, but I will later use the output for Gene Set Enrichment Analysis (GSEA), which also requires values for lowly expressed genes. Therefore, I run FindAllMarkers() with loose thresholds (`logfc.threshold = 0` and `min.pct = 0.1`). Results of top markers are displayed below, using the function `top_markers()` which I defined above. I also saved a csv with the full results on disk, so I could inspect the full list myself.

```{r}
#| label: chunk-19-findmarkers
# Run FindAllMarkers, but with very loose thresholds: I'll run GSEA of GO-terms
# on it, which means I'll want a gene score of almost all genes
markers <- FindAllMarkers(
  seu,
  logfc.threshold = 0,
  min.pct = 0.1
)

## Extract a table of top markers and save full table to disk
# I put top markers per cluster in a list to later display it as a tabset
list_markers <- list()
# Extract the number of clusters present in each resolution
marker_levels <- markers |>
  distinct(cluster) |>
  mutate(cluster = as.numeric(as.character(cluster)))
# The previous step created a dataframe, so select the column 'cluster'
for (i in marker_levels$cluster) {
  # Extract table of top markers and store in list
  list_entry_name <- paste0("Cluster ", i)
  list_markers[[list_entry_name]] <- top_markers(markers, cluster_select = i)
  # Write to disk as csv
  file_csv <- paste0("markers_", res, "_cluster", i, ".csv")
  file_csv <- file.path(dir_tab, file_csv)
  markers |>
    filter(cluster == i) |>
    write_csv(file_csv, col_names = TRUE, quote = "none")
}
```

### Grey matter-white matter astrocyte distinction

Another distinction I could quickly make was a division in grey matter and white matter astrocytes. This dataset was annotated using reference atlases, and the atlas from the Allen Brain institue provided a white matter-grey matter astrocyte distinction. This aligns well with cluster 1 vs cluster 2 and 3. I therefore labelled cluster 1 grey matter (GM) astrocytes and cluster 2 and 3 white matter (WM) astrocytes.

```{r}
#| label: fig-05-allen-wm-gm

  "WM Astrocytes" = "#80CDC1",
  "GM Astrocytes"   = "#DFC27D"
)

p_allen <- DimPlot(
  seu, 
  reduction = "umap", 
  group.by = "predicted.id_coarse_allen_group",
  cols = cols_allen,
  pt.size = 2,
  alpha = 1,
  raster = TRUE # Rasterized as I use this figure in my manuscript
  ) +
  labs(x = "UMAP1", y = "UMAP2")
p_allen + theme_quarto()
```

```{r}
#| echo: false

          legend_pos_manuscript = "right")

```

I came to the same conclusion using GO-terms. To test enrichment of pathways, I loaded in GO terms with the `msigdbr` package and used GO:Biological Processes (GO:BP). The Seurat object contacts both genes given with SYMBOL and with EnsebmlID. SYMBOL genes are the standard, the EnsembleID genes in our data are either lnc-RNAs, transcript isoforms or other things - which are not in the GO:BP anyways. These are thus removed from the analysis. I can run GO terms both by logFC and p-value. Both have their benefits and downsides. Good to say that it these GO-terms thus are exploratory. For now only on fold change (mostly based on this discussion: https://github.com/alserglab/fgsea/issues/50), but I wrote the function `prepare_gsea()` to also be able to use signed-log10(p); I test this below as well.

```{r}
#| label: chunk-23-markers-goterms-clust-1-3
# Load in the gene set using msigdbr::msigdbr()
gs_go_bp <- msigdbr(
  species = "Homo sapiens", 
  collection = "C5", 
  subcollection = "GO:BP"
)
# Adapt the gene set to the input required for fgsea: it needs to be a list 
# with your pathways/gene set names and the genes that make up each pathway.
gene_sets <- split(x = gs_go_bp$gene_symbol, f = gs_go_bp$gs_name)

# Run GSEA for all clusters. For each cluster: save the output-table on disk and
# create a visualization. Use a list to store all visualizations.
# I would manually set clusters with marker_levels$cluster, so it works
# automatically, but that would include cluster 4, still, so I'll set it
# with 1:3
plot_list <- list()
for (i in 1:3) {
  gene_scores <- prepare_gsea(
    markers, 
    findallmarkers = TRUE, 
    identity = i, 
    sort = "logfc"
    )

  # Run GSEA with the fgsea package
  gsea_res <- fgsea(
    pathways = gene_sets, # List of gene sets to check
    stats = gene_scores,
    scoreType = 'std', # std as we have both pos and neg rankings
    minSize = 10, # otherwise I only get pathways with 2-5 genes
    maxSize = 500,
  )
  
  file_csv <- file.path(dir_tab, paste0("goterms_", res, "_cluster", i, ".csv"))
  write_csv(gsea_res, file_csv, col_names = TRUE, quote = "none")
  
  ## Create a visualization
  top_pathways <- gsea_pathway_selection(
    gsea_res, 
    n_up = number_of_top_pathways_up,
    n_down = number_of_top_pathways_down
    )
  
  p_gsea <- plotGseaTable(
    gene_sets[top_pathways], 
    stats = gene_scores, 
    fgseaRes = gsea_res, 
    headerLabelStyle = list(size = 14),
    pathwayLabelStyle = list(size = 12),
    valueStyle = list(size = 10),
    gseaParam = 0.5 # Makes the figure clearer
    )
  # Store the plot in the list under the name of the cluster
  list_entry_name <- paste0("Cluster ", i)
  plot_list[[list_entry_name]] <- p_gsea
}

```

If we examine the GO terms for which cluster 3 is enriched, we see that these are GO terms such as synaptic signalling, Neurotransmitter transport and other terms associated with synapse function. Previous studies described that this describes neuron-interacting or Grey Matter astrocytes.

# Cell composition analysis

I will now examine cell composition. (Explain what cell composition is) with scCODA. The first part is done in R: I need to prepare it in a tidy format from my seurat object. I will then perfrom the statistical test with scCODA, which is in Python, and provide visualizations back in R with ggplot2 (ggplot2 over matplotlib any day of the week), for which I defined the function `boxplot_composition()`.

First create a count table. ggplot2 and scCODA require slightly different input: for ggplot, I need to pivot_longer. I'll do that in the bar_freq function

```{r}
#| label: chunk-36-count-table-cell-comp
metadata <- seu@meta.data

# Select columns to test
col_selection <- c(
  "AnonymousID", 
  "condition",
  "Gender", 
  "primary_site_of_onset", 
  "pTDP43_lumped", 
  "disease.subtype"
)

# Create a metadata table which only has one row per participant
metadata_sample <- metadata |>
  distinct(AnonymousID, .keep_all = TRUE) |>
  select(all_of(col_selection))

# Create a count table of the astrocyte clusters and join it with the sample
# metadata
cell_counts <- metadata |>
  count(AnonymousID, annotation) |>
  pivot_wider(
    names_from = annotation,
    values_from = n,
    values_fill = 0 # scCODA needs 0 in stead of NA
  ) |>
  inner_join(
    metadata_sample,
    by = join_by(AnonymousID)
  ) |>
  rename(disease_subtype = disease.subtype) # otherwise a Python error
```

scCODA is a Python package. Fortunately, Quarto allows you to use R and Python within the same document (that's partly why I chose to use Quarto). I can let R and Python interact via the R package `reticulate`, so I'll first need to configure `reticulate`. The `RETICULATE_PYTHON` variable was set in the bash script which runs this script via a slurm job, and is configured to python in the conda environment `py_scrnaseq`.

```{r}
#| label: chunk-37-reticulate-configure
# Adapted so it does not print my directory
basename(dirname(dirname(Sys.getenv("RETICULATE_PYTHON"))))
```


```{python}
#| label: chunk-38-sccoda-prerequisites

import warnings
warnings.filterwarnings("ignore")

import pandas as pd

from sccoda.util import comp_ana as mod
from sccoda.util import cell_composition_data as dat
```

This chunk runs it for condition (ALS vs Ctrls), click below to see chunks which run it for other variables

```{python}
#| label: chunk-39-sccoda-condition

cellcounts = r.cell_counts
variable = "condition"

# Provide which columns are variables
var_cols = [
    "AnonymousID",
    "condition",
    "Gender", 
    "primary_site_of_onset", 
    "pTDP43_lumped", 
    "disease_subtype"
    ]

data = dat.from_pandas(cellcounts, covariate_columns= var_cols)

model = mod.CompositionalAnalysis(
    data, 
    formula = variable, 
    reference_cell_type = "automatic"
    )

results = model.sample_hmc(verbose = False)

print(results.summary())
print(results.credible_effects())

```
Visualize with ggplot2:

```{r}
#| label: fig-13-cell-comp-condition
cols_condition <- c("Ctrl" = "#0072B2", "ALS" = "#D55E00")

p_bar_con <- boxplot_composition(cell_counts, variable = "condition")  +
  scale_fill_manual(values = cols_condition) +
  labs(x = "")
p_bar_con + theme_quarto(legend_position = "top")
```
